sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent closed-source image generation systems can produce diverse visual content from simple compositions to information-dense graphics, yet open-weight text-to-image models still struggle with dense text and intricate layouts. To narrow this gap, we introduce MOSS-Image, an open generation system that combines high-fidelity visual synthesis with intent-aware composition. First, we pretrain a 5B single-stream diffusion transformer (DiT) from scratch with a carefully designed recipe, enabling bilingual long-form text rendering and precise layout control. Second, we develop an intention-aware agentic prompt enhancement (PE) module that translates diverse user requests into detailed content and layout specifications. Together, they enable MOSS-Image to generate text-rich and layout-coherent images. We further introduce LongLongTextBench (LLTB) for evaluating long-form English and Chinese text rendering, and RealLayoutArena (RLA) for end-to-end layout-rich generation. MOSS-Image achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-weight models on LLTB, with an average text coverage of 96.3%. On RLA, MOSS-Image ranks second in the end-to-end system comparison, while its backbone ranks first among generators evaluated with shared enhanced prompts. We will release the model, training recipe, and evaluation framework to support further research and promote the text-to-image community.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Text-to-image (T2I) foundation models have made substantial progress in visual quality, semantic alignment, and text rendering in recent years. Proprietary systems, such as GPT Image 2 [1], Seedream 5.0 Pro [2], Qwen Image 3.0 Pro [3], and Nano Banana Pro [4] have extended image generation from artistic creation to practical visual communication, such as infographics, user interfaces, and knowledge cards. Open-weight models, including Stable Diffusion [5], SDXL [6], FLUX [7], Qwen-Image [8], Z-Image [9], ERNIE-Image [10], and Boogu-Image [11], have made these capabilities increasingly accessible, yet they still struggle with dense text and intricate layouts. For such graphics, plausible overall appearance does not guarantee legible text, complete content, or coherent spatial organization (Figure 1). At the same time, concise request may specify only topic and format, leaving the actual content, information hierarchy, and spatial organization to be developed. We attribute this gap to two coupled challenges: rendering and specification. Rendering involves accurately Full contributors can be found in the Contributors section. 1 Figure 1 Complex graphic generation from concise user request. The examples illustrate differences in content, composition, and text rendering across generation configurations. MOSS-Image combines pretrained diffusion transformer with prompt enhancement and optional explicit layout specifications. The proprietary output provides visual reference; quantitative comparisons are reported in Section 5. reproducing long text and following spatial constraints. Specification involves translating concise user request into content and layout instructions, with level of detail appropriate to the request. Neither capability alone is sufficient: detailed specifications do not guarantee faithful rendering, while rendering ability alone does not resolve the content and design decisions left unspecified by the user. This calls for system that connects intent-aware specification with faithful rendering, and for evaluation that assesses the resulting designs end to end. To address these issues, we present MOSS-Image, which pairs text-and-layout-capable generator with an agent that enriches sparse requests and designs deliberate layouts. On the generation side, we pretrain 5B single-stream diffusion transformer (DiT) from scratch for dense bilingual text and multi-element graphics. Its recipe combines broad data retention, multi-granularity and structure-aware textual supervision, and progressive-resolution training; crucially, natural-language descriptions and explicit layout specifications are learned through single text-conditioning pathway, so the model can follow either form. On the composition side, we develop an intention-aware agentic prompt enhancement (PE) module that routes each request to task-specific guidance and retrieves knowledge and visual references as needed. Unlike such generator-agnostic agents [12], which can only communicate through natural-language prompts, our enhancer turns brief requests into structured layouts that the DiT follows for precise composition control. To evaluate rendering, we introduce LongLongTextBench (LLTB) for long-form English and Chinese text, complementing LongTextBench and 7Bench. These benchmarks assess the execution of specified text or spatial constraints, but do not measure whether complete system can select and organize content into coherent design from concise user request. We therefore introduce RealLayoutArena (RLA) to evaluate end-to-end generation of complex graphics from short design requests. Since request can admit multiple valid designs, RLA uses blind pairwise human comparisons to jointly assess instruction following, content completeness, text readability, and visual organization. We further conduct prompt-strategy ablations and cross-backbone comparisons under shared enhanced prompts to disentangle the roles of specification and generator. 2 On LLTB, MOSS-Image achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-weight models with Mean-6 score of 96.3, surpassing Qwen Image 2512 (64.9) by 31.4 percentage points. On RLA, MOSS-Image achieves 1698.70 Elo, ranking second in the end-to-end comparison, behind GPT Image 2 and ahead of Seedream 5.0 Pro. With shared enhanced natural-language prompts, our backbone achieves the highest rating at 1807.34 Elo. Prompt comparisons further show that detailed specifications substantially improve human preference over concise requests. Our contributions are summarized as follows: pretrained foundation model for information-dense graphics. We develop 5B diffusion transformer pretrained from scratch that demonstrates strong bilingual long-form text rendering and layout control through unified text-conditioning interface. We detail its pretraining recipe, including broad data retention, multi-granularity and structure-aware textual supervision, and progressive-resolution training, providing practical foundation for further research on complex graphic generation. An agentic end-to-end generation system. We build MOSS-Image by pairing the foundation model with an intention-aware agentic prompt enhancer that translates diverse user requests, even those of fewer than ten words, into detailed, executable generation specifications. Through task-specific routing, knowledge and visual reference retrieval, and structured layout planning, the system produces graphics that remain faithful to user intent while adapting their information density to what each request calls for, from minimalist designs to information-rich layouts. Benchmarks and systematic analysis. We introduce LLTB, which evaluates bilingual text rendering under extended text lengths, and RLA, which evaluates complex graphic generation under realistic user requests at the system level. MOSS-Image achieves state-of-the-art open-weight performance on LLTB (96.3 Mean-6), ranks second in the end-to-end RLA comparison, and attains the highest rating under shared enhanced prompts. Prompt comparisons further assess the effects of content and layout details.

sections.title: 2 System Overview
sections.content: MOSS-Image pairs pretrained text-and-layout generator with an intent-aware prompt enhancer (Figure 2). The enhancer turns concise request into content and layout specification; the generator renders that specification into an image. Text and layout rendering. To render long text and follow spatial constraints, we pretrain 5B single-stream DiT from scratch. Natural-language descriptions and structured layouts share one text-conditioning pathway. Broad data retention, multi-granularity and structure-aware supervision, and progressive training build this capability. Section 3 details the model pretraining recipe. Intent-aware prompt enhancement. To resolve the content and design choices left unspecified by short request, an agent selects task-specific guidance, retrieves knowledge and visual references as needed, and constructs detailed generation specifications. Its layout output uses the same textual interface learned by the generator. Section 4 describes this inference-time module.

sections.title: 3.1 Pretraining Corpus Construction
sections.content: We construct the corpus from ReLAION [15], OmniCorpus [16], DataComp [17], and additional public image-text datasets. Following source-specific build preprocessing, corpus preparation uses SSCD-based deduplication [18] and removal of AI-generated images using an in-house detector, reducing the corpus from 4 Figure 3 Pretraining recipe of MOSS-Image. (a) After deduplication and AI-image removal, we keep all images and caption their artifacts instead of filtering them out. (b) ReLAION sample with its original caption, three recaptions, and layout JSON (excerpts); the JSONs object and text boxes are drawn in orange and blue. Visible text, marked in blue, is transcribed verbatim, line breaks () included. (c) Maximum tokens per sample in each stage. approximately 5 billion to 3 billion images. We mix data sources in their original proportions. No additional data filtering. At this subsequent corpus-preparation stage, we apply no further filtering beyond deduplication and AI-image removal; this does not exclude quality filters already applied during source builds, such as the ReLAION NSFW and watermark checks. This is deliberate pretraining choice, supported by preliminary filtering experiments, to retain broad visual coverage. Residual attributes such as watermarks, blurry faces, and compression artifacts are incorporated into the textual supervision rather than used as exclusion criteria. Appendix provides dataset details, and Appendix B.2 describes the preliminary experiments. (cid:17) Annotate rather than filter. We advocate preserving real-world data distributions by annotating undesirable attributes rather than filtering out images.

3.2 Multi-granularity and Structure-aware Supervision
Descriptions at multiple granularities. We caption images with gemma4 [19] at different semantic granularities:
a short sentence, a medium paragraph, or a detailed description of composition, subjects, scene attributes,
and visible text. These variants are defined by content rather than fixed token budgets. Training samples

sections.content: Explicit text and structure. For subset of images, we additionally construct structured annotations containing global descriptions and localized elements with bounding boxes, categories, and, where applicable, transcribed text and typography attributes. The documented annotation recipes validate JSON structure and coordinate constraints. During training, annotations are geometrically aligned and optional fields undergo stochastic dropout before serialization through the text-conditioning interface in Section 2. Appendix C.2 describes annotation checks, and Appendix C.3 details the schemas and preprocessing policies. Preserving line structure. We preserve line breaks in annotated text to match its arrangement in the image. 3.3 Pretraining Schedule and Optimization
Progressive training. Training increases image resolution and text-context capacity across three stages (Table 1).
The final stage preserves aspect ratio, aligns image dimensions to multiples of 16, and caps target image area
at 10242 pixels. We concatenate the condition fields, apply the Qwen chat template, and tokenize with a
final-stage limit of 4096 text tokens.
sections.content: Caption sampling ratios. We mix original captions with multi-granularity recaptions. In the standard caption branch, original captions and recaptions are sampled at 20:80 ratio when both are available, with uniform selection among valid recaption variants (1:1:1 for short/medium/long when all three are present). Missing alternatives fall back to available descriptions. We additionally annotate selected subset of high-quality data with layout descriptions, serialized as bbox JSON, to provide explicit text and spatial supervision. These structured annotations are sampled according to domain-specific policies and annotation availability. Appendix C.1 provides the details. (cid:17) Detailed annotations raise the performance ceiling; diverse annotations preserve generalization. RoPE design. Preliminary ablations (Appendix D) show similar overall image-generation performance across RoPE coordinate assignments, with trade-offs across metrics. We retain dedicated reference-index axis 𝑟 to allow future extensions to reference-conditioned generation. In the current setting without reference inputs, all tokens use 𝑟 = 0, so its associated feature subspace remains unrotated, while the other axes encode sequence and spatial positions. This supports more references without changing the positional encoding. Muon and convergence efficiency. We choose hybrid MuonAdamW for its sustained convergence advantage, applying Muon to eligible matrices and AdamW to the remaining parameters throughout pretraining. Our 1B ablation shows lower denoising loss in both early and late training, reaching losses of 0.41 and 0.403 with 33.2% and 28.6% fewer steps than AdamW, respectively. Appendix reports the convergence curves and measurement protocol; final training settings are given in Appendix A.2.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup and Benchmarks
sections.content: We separate evaluation of the pretrained generator from evaluation of complete generation systems. LongTextBench [20] and LLTB measure bilingual text rendering, while 7Bench [21] measures layout control. These evaluations use the MOSS-Image backbone without our agentic prompt enhancer. RLA evaluates complete systems on concise design requests. Baseline scores on LongTextBench are collected from public 7 reports, whereas all results on 7Bench, LLTB, and RLA are obtained through our own evaluation. Benchmark construction, generation settings, and evaluation protocols are specified in Appendix G. LongTextBench saturation. The collected LongTextBench results cluster between 96.05 and 98.85 overall (Appendix G.4). We therefore consider LongTextBench close to saturation for current strong models under its text-coverage metric. Its targets average only 120.3 characters  (Table 2)  ; near-ceiling scores on these relatively short targets offer limited discrimination of sustained long-text rendering ability. We retain the detailed results in the appendix and emphasize longer text conditions in our main evaluation. LongLongTextBench. We construct 240 literary-text rendering tasks, with 120 each in English and Chinese and three body-length bins. Table 2 compares the two benchmarks: LLTB averages 1,339.8 characters per target, approximately 11.1 LongTextBench, and contains 321,545 characters in total, approximately 8.4 as many. Its shortest target (444 characters) already approaches LongTextBenchs longest (482), shifting the evaluation toward dense, page-length text. We reuse the LongTextBench OCR and word/character multiset-recall metric. Coverage is computed within each languagelength group and averaged equally across the six groups (Mean-6). Construction and scoring details are given in Appendix G.1. RealLayoutArena. We construct 61 tasks from manually selected design references: 20 posters, 20 infographics, and 21 user interfaces. Raters compare two outputs for the same short request, with model names hidden, considering instruction following, rendering quality, and spatial organization. We fit BradleyTerry ratings on an Elo scale with asymptotic 95% confidence intervals; ties and both bad count as half-wins. Appendix G.2 details the protocol.

sections.title: 5.2 Base DiT Evaluation
sections.content: We first evaluate capabilities acquired by the pretrained backbone independently of our prompt enhancement pipeline. These results characterize the resulting model; they do not isolate the causal contribution of individual pretraining choices. Text rendering. We emphasize LLTB to assess rendering under substantially longer text conditions  (Table 4)  ; supplementary LongTextBench results are reported in Appendix G.4. MOSS-Image obtains 96.3 Mean-6 on LLTB, the highest score among the open-weight models listed in the table. Its scores on the longest English and Chinese conditions are 97.1 and 92.4, respectively. Text recall is high overall but lower for the longest Chinese texts. Layout control. Table 3 reports mean IoU over detected target objects (mIoUdet) and Layout AUC. MOSSImage achieves 0.88 and 0.70, respectively, compared with 0.44 and 0.20 for Ideogram 4, leading all evaluated models on both metrics. These results demonstrate precise object placement through the text-conditioning interface. Appendix G.4 details the evaluation protocol, filtered outputs, detection rates, and results including undetected objects.

sections.title: 6 Case Study
sections.content: Layout-Guided Zero-Shot Modification. Modifying the layout prompt enables targeted content replacement and element rearrangement while retaining the overall design. These changes are achieved through text-to-image regeneration without conditioning on the original image or additional training. Qualitative examples are provided in Appendix I. Line-Break Alignment in Text Annotations. We observe that prompts with explicit line breaks help the model establish the character content of each line earlier and more readily during denoising, leading to better final text rendering. Appendix provides qualitative comparison. 9 Bounding-Box Coordinate Representations. We observe that zero-centered absolute bounding-box coordinates generalize better to resolutions unseen during training than relative coordinates normalized to [0, 1000]. Appendix provides qualitative comparison.

sections.title: 8 Limitations
sections.content: The current MOSS-Image backbone supports text-to-image generation but does not directly condition on reference images or support image editing. Extending the model to image-conditioned generation and iterative design refinement would broaden its use in creative workflows; these capabilities remain future work under our current computational budget. The prompt enhancer relies on external language models, whose limitations in aesthetic judgment, reference interpretation, and factual errors can reduce specification quality despite faithful rendering.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: We present MOSS-Image, an open complex graphic generation system built around 5B diffusion transformer pretrained from scratch. Its training recipe combines broad image-text data, multi-granularity and structureaware supervision, and multi-stage resolution training. The resulting backbone supports strong bilingual long-form text rendering and layout control, while an agentic prompt enhancer translates concise requests into detailed generation specifications. LLTB and RLA evaluate rendering capability and complete-system performance, complemented by prompt-strategy and shared-prompt cross-backbone comparisons. MOSS-Image achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-weight models on LLTB with Mean-6 score of 96.3. On RLA, MOSS-Image ranks second in the end-to-end comparison, while its backbone achieves the highest rating under shared enhanced natural-language prompts. The prompt comparisons show that supplying detailed content and design instructions improves human preference over concise requests. Together, these results support combining capable renderer with explicit generation specifications for complex graphics.

C.1 Caption Generation and Sampling We generate short, medium, and long descriptions to provide multi-granularity textual supervision, and sample among the available captions during training. Generation recipe. We generate three complementary descriptions for each image: short single-sentence summary, medium paragraph condensed from the long description, and detailed account of composition, subjects, actions, environment, and style. The three levels differ in semantic detail rather than fixed token or word counts. Caption generation is conditioned on the image, its original caption, and descriptive perspective. Visible text is transcribed without translation or transliteration, preserving line breaks, reading order, location, alignment, font, color, and spacing. Availability and observed lengths. We characterize caption lengths using 5,792 images sampled across 94 data shards, with up to 64 uniformly spaced images per shard. Of these, 4,335 contain complete short/medium/long triplet. Table 11 reports token-length statistics for these triplets using the Qwen3.5-9B tokenizer, excluding special tokens, training prefixes, and layout annotations, and without truncation. The longest sampled long caption contains 3,126 tokens. The statistics describe this annotation sample. Variant Mean P10 Median P90 Short Medium Long 20.86 76.61 235.12 16 59 153 20 75 193 26 97 293 18 Conditional sampling. When both an original caption and generated caption are available, we select the generated caption with probability 0.8; otherwise, we use the available source. We then sample uniformly among its nonempty descriptions, assigning probability 1/3 to each length when all three are present. C.2 Annotation Validation Caption validation checks JSON syntax and the presence of three nonempty descriptions. Layout validation checks required fields, four-integer bounding boxes, coordinate ranges, positive box area, unique element identifiers, parent references, and color formats. The Gemmaand Qwen-based annotation generators allow up to three retries for invalid outputs. These checks enforce the annotation structure; the coordinate transformations and field selection used for textual conditioning are described in Appendix C.3. C.3 Conditioning Schemas and Coordinate Conventions The structured annotation pipeline supports two main schema families: scene/element and summary/items. Both combine global descriptions with localized content and bounding boxes. Figure 6 illustrates the two formats; supplementary format appends item-level annotations to natural-language caption. Scene/element schema. The scene/element format combines scene category and global brief with composition metadata, localized elements, spatial anchors, and palette. Object elements describe identity and appearance; text elements specify visible text, typography, and watermark status. The stored boxes use [𝑦1, 𝑥1, 𝑦2, 𝑥2] coordinates normalized to [0, 1000]. Training transforms boxes to match the image geometry and samples normalized, absolute-pixel, or center-relative pixel coordinates with probabilities 0.4/0.3/0.3 within this branch. The normalized cases are split equally between implicit and explicit coordinate-format markers. For transformed image of height 𝐻 and width 𝑊, center-relative pixel boxes are [𝑦1 𝐻/2, 𝑥1 𝑊/2, 𝑦2 𝐻/2, 𝑥2 𝑊/2], where (𝑥, 𝑦) are pixel coordinates after geometric transformation. Optional fields are dropped and element order is randomized, while gen_brief and elements are retained  (Table 12)  . Summary/items schema. The summary/items format contains global summary and localized items, labeled as panels, objects, characters, text, or watermarks. We convert provider-specific box conventions to normalized [0, 1000] 𝑦𝑥𝑦𝑥 coordinates and transform them consistently with image resizing, cropping, and flipping. Fully cropped or degenerate items are removed. Element identifiers and parent references are discarded, leaving the localized descriptions and spatial coordinates as the structural condition. Summary fields and item attributes undergo the stochastic transformations in Table 12. The serialized condition is processed by the shared text encoder. Supplementary item-level conditions and sampling. supplementary condition appends item-level boxes, labels, tags, and captions to base natural-language description, together with coordinate-system marker. sections.content: F.1 GPT-6 Planner and Task Guidance We use GPT-6 as planner with shared instructions for constraint extraction, text preservation, composition, readability, and structured output. Task-specific guidance covers posters, infographics, and user interfaces  (Table 14)  . Routing prioritizes the medium explicitly requested by the user, followed by the inferred communication goal. For example, an educational poster follows the poster route unless an infographic is explicitly requested. User-specified content, literal strings, language, and canvas dimensions constrain the resulting plan. Planner sessions. The final Layout PE plans each task in an independent session. An earlier version planned all 61 RLA tasks within single shared context. The main system uses the final version, while the prompt-strategy ablation and the shared-prompt generator comparison use the earlier version. Table 14 Task-specific planning guidance for the prompt enhancer. Suggested reference counts are adapted to the request and the available material. Route Poster Infographic User interface Planning priorities Reference guidance Information hierarchy, complete event or campaign content, typography, and coherent visual composition. Develop factual explanations jointly with diagrams, labels, and reading order; preserve substantive content when grouping elements. Match the intended page, platform, viewport, version, and populated interface state. Search same-theme posters; typically inspect 35 distinct examples and compare content, density, and typography/layout. Inspect relevant visual references and consult authoritative sources for unfamiliar or uncertain facts. Collect roughly 36 candidates and normally inspect at least 3 distinct screenshots; prefer 2 sources and 2 relevant page views when available. The planner is instructed to retrieve relevant material through web and image search and visually inspect candidate references. The guidance recommends 13 focused queries and 24 useful images, with task-specific guidance as listed in Table 14. For user interfaces, the search can be refined to match the requested page, platform, and populated state. Retrieved designs inform composition and appearance, while unfamiliar factual content is checked against authoritative sources. For broad knowledge graphics, the infographic guidance suggests 69 substantive modules, 2236 knowledge units, and approximately 300500 visible English words on 1024 (14001600) canvas. The planner adjusts these targets to the requested scope, language, canvas, and readability. Related content is grouped into coherent visual units, with the number of elements determined by the design. F.2 Structured Prompt Format The planner returns one JSON object with eight root fields: scene_type, gen_brief, aspect_ratio, layout, elements, anchors, must_not, and palette. Compared with the representative scene/element training schema in Appendix C.3, the inference format additionally includes aspect_ratio and must_not. 23 The global brief uses 60120 English words; layout specifies composition and viewpoint. Elements use type=obj or type=text; object salience distinguishes primary and secondary roles. Type-specific fields encode appearance, literal copy, color, and placement. Every visible string is written literally in text element, preserving the users original characters and intended line breaks. Descriptive fields are in English. Related strings and mixed typography may share box when their internal organization remains explicit. Up to three anchors encode important spatial relationships, and up to three must_not entries describe concrete, request-specific visual exclusions. The planner emits integer boxes in normalized [0, 1000] coordinates with top-left origin and order [𝑦min, 𝑥min, 𝑦max, 𝑥max]. It requires positive box width and height and allows overlap when implied by the intended composition. For output dimensions 𝑊 𝐻, the planner checks text fit using the physical box dimensions Δ𝑥 𝑊/1000 and Δ𝑦 𝐻/1000, literal line breaks, and typography hierarchy. Boxes describe coherent visual units, not mandatory visible panels. F.3 Specification Validation Before returning specification, the planner is instructed to check JSON syntax, required fields, coordinate validity, literal text, and consistency between the global composition and localized elements. Task-specific checks cover content completeness and readability. Intended line breaks are represented as escaped newline characters in JSON. Reference information is incorporated into self-contained visual descriptions, while research notes and source URLs are kept outside the image-description fields.

sections.title: L Related Work
sections.content: Foundation models and pretraining. Latent diffusion [5] and diffusion transformers [37] underpin modern image generation. SDXL [6], Stable Diffusion 3 [38], FLUX [7], Qwen-Image [8], Z-Image [9], and ERNIEImage [10] advance general-purpose synthesis and instruction following. Qwen-Image-2.1 [39] further unifies image generation and editing with compact 7B visual generator, improved typography, and native support for transparent images. SenseNova-U1.5 [40] pursues native unified visual understanding and generation through an encoder-free and VAE-free architecture, with advances in bilingual text rendering, infographic generation, and complex composition. Training recipes are also central: PixArt-𝛼 [41] emphasizes informative captions and staged training, while Z-Image combines data curation, multi-level captions, and progressive training. Building on this direction, MOSS-Image documents the corpus, multi-granularity and structure-aware supervision, and resolution schedule used to pretrain 5B generator, with focus on bilingual long-form text and complex graphics. Visual text generation. GlyphControl [42] and TextDiffuser [43] use glyph or character-level guidance to improve text rendering. AnyText [44] extends controlled rendering to multiple languages, and AnyText2 [45] adds customizable font and color attributes. TextDiffuser-2 [46] further uses language models for layout planning and line-level text-position encoding, while Qwen-Image [8] incorporates strong text rendering into general-purpose model. These advances motivate our study of long passages within dense, multi-element graphics, where character fidelity and overall composition must be evaluated together. Layout-conditioned generation. ControlNet [47] and T2I-Adapter [48] introduce spatial control through auxiliary conditioning modules; GLIGEN [49], LayoutDiffusion [50], and BoxDiff [51] explore grounding, layout-aware modeling, and training-free box constraints, respectively. FIBO [52] improves compositional control through long structured captions with descriptive spatial fields, while MOSS-Image additionally 34 supports explicit bounding-box coordinates. Spatial alignment alone, however, does not establish accurate long-form text rendering. Closely related concurrent work, Ideogram 4 [36], trains on structured JSON captions with text and layout descriptions, supports bounding-box control and LLM-based prompt expansion, and reports text-rendering and layout results. Its public weight release is limited to FP8/NF4 quantized checkpoints, accompanied by inference code but not complete pretraining recipe. Our work documents corpus construction, supervision design, and the training schedule for 5B generator targeting bilingual long passages and dense graphic layouts. LLTB and RLA assess rendering under extended text lengths and complete-system performance, respectively. Prompt enhancement and image agents. Promptist [53] learns to adapt user inputs to model-preferred prompts, and Z-Image [9] incorporates reasoning-based prompt enhancement. Concurrent Qwen-Image-Agent [12] constructs generation context through planning, reasoning, search, memory, and feedback, including layoutaware content planning. Its training-free framework operates over existing image generators. MOSS-Image combines agent-produced layout specifications with newly pretrained backbone that learns from textrich data and explicit text-and-structure supervision. Our distinction concerns training the renderer and connecting it to structured layout specifications; prompt-strategy and cross-backbone comparisons examine how these components affect the outputs. Evaluation of text-rich graphics. GenEval [54] and T2I-CompBench [55] assess compositional alignment. MARIO-Eval [43], AnyText-benchmark [44], and LongTextBench [20] target visual text, while 7Bench [21] evaluates layout-guided generation and IA-Bench [12] tests image-agent capabilities. Our LLTB extends bilingual text rendering to longer passages, and RLA evaluates content, layout, and text quality jointly for complete systems responding to realistic graphic-design requests.
